The data review for leadership: the depth treatment

1. Two Mondays, two rooms

On Monday 13 October 2025, Nandita Varkey, Chief Product Officer of Bahipatra Systems, a Pune company selling warehouse execution software to large Indian retailers and 3PLs, had ninety minutes before a quarterly business review with her chief executive, her chief revenue officer and two non-executive directors. The number on the agenda came from Bahipatra's Series C deck: plan completion rate, the share of replenishment plans started in a week that reach a despatch instruction. It had sat between 70 and 72 per cent for five quarters; in the week ending 10 October it printed 67.7. The CRO had already emailed a theory: the product had got harder to use since the September release.

Nandita had spent the weekend with her head of analytics, Ismail Qureshi, and knew something the CRO did not: plan completion had improved in every segment Bahipatra tracked, enterprise and mid-market alike, and the company-wide number had still fallen three points. Her question was not what to investigate, but what a single page should say when the true finding is that the metric on the board deck is, this quarter, not measuring the product at all.

Two thousand kilometres away, Aakash Bhattacharya, Head of Product at Roznamcha, a Gurugram company whose assistant turns a field agent's voice note into a structured insurance or crop-loan record, was preparing a different page. Roznamcha had shipped a new model, v5, on 8 September. Since then the metric on every wall — accepted-without-edit rate, the share of generated records an agent submits untouched — had climbed from 64 to 71 per cent. The weekly audit, in which a two-person quality team in Kochi checks four hundred submitted records against source documents, moved the other way: verified accuracy of accepted records had fallen from 92.5 to 88.0 per cent. Roznamcha's largest customer was an agri-lender regulated by the Reserve Bank of India, and an inaccurate record in a disbursement file is not a usability defect. Aakash's chief executive had spent the week telling investors that v5 lifted adoption seven points.

Both pages are the same artefact under two kinds of pressure. Nandita must tell a room that the number it governs by is arithmetically misleading; Aakash must tell a room that the number it celebrates is moving the wrong way in the only sense that matters. Neither can write a longer document; neither room will read one.

2. The idea, and the traditions that disagree about it

A data review for leadership is a single written page, addressed to a named decision-making body, that states what changed in a metric that body governs by, decomposes the change into causes with a number attached to each and an honest residual, records the action with an owner and a date, and states the one thing the author needs. It reports a root-cause analysis; it is not one. The analysis establishes mechanism and can be audited; the review is the decision object built on it, and the discipline is in what it refuses to carry.

The form has four intellectual parents that do not agree. Barbara Minto's pyramid, developed inside McKinsey from 1967, insists a document lead with its answer. Variance analysis, from the cost accounting of DuPont and General Motors in the 1920s, supplies the machinery for splitting a movement into components that sum to the total. Statistical process control — Walter Shewhart at Bell Labs in 1924, later W. Edwards Deming — supplies the prior question: is this a signal, or the ordinary variation of a stable process? Deming's funnel experiment, showing that responding to common-cause variation makes a process worse, is the most under-applied idea in product reviews. And the narrative-memo tradition, from Grove's operations reviews at Intel and Amazon's 2004 replacement of decks with memos read in silence, makes the page the meeting itself.

Four positions descend from these, and argument is clarified by asking which proposition each would sign. The narrative school treats the review as a written argument that must survive a hostile cold reading. It signs "an analyst who cannot write the finding as prose has not finished the analysis." It will not sign "the purpose of the review is to record commitments," because it treats the page as an instrument of thinking rather than accountability.

The control school, descending from Shewhart through modern site-reliability practice, holds that most weekly movements are noise and that narrating noise is the central pathology of the business review. It signs "the correct response to a movement inside control limits is to say nothing," and will not sign "every material change deserves an explanation," because materiality to a board and statistical distinguishability are different tests.

The accountability school, descending from Grove, holds that the review exists to close loops: last period's commitment, this period's variance, next period's owner. It signs "a review without an owner and a date is theatre," and will not sign "the review's primary purpose is to inform."

The calibration school, from decision analysis and forecasting research, holds that a review must carry an explicit confidence and a falsifier — the observation that would have changed the author's mind. It signs "an attribution without a confidence is a guess wearing a suit," and will not sign "hedged language slows leaders down," which is precisely what the other schools say about it. Most practice is an unstable blend of all four.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice runs a sequence whose first two steps are invisible in the finished page, which is why they are skipped most often.

Step zero: establish that there is something to review

The expert first asks whether a movement is distinguishable from the metric's own week-to-week variation. Bahipatra's weekly active planner count ran across weeks 29 to 39 at 4,740, 4,805, 4,690, 4,830, 4,770, 4,715, 4,880, 4,760, 4,795, 4,720 and 4,820 — mean 4,775, standard deviation about 57, three-sigma limits at roughly 4,603 and 4,947. In week 40 it printed 4,305: more than eight standard deviations out.

Two second-order points follow. Control limits on a growing product are wrong by construction, because the process is not stationary; the expert detrends first, charting residuals against the recent growth rate. And a published chart changes the politics of the review: once limits exist, "the number moved" no longer compels an explanation, and the author acquires standing to say a movement is not worth a page — worth more over a year than any single well-written review.

Step one: decompose, and make the parts sum

The formal treatment separating expert reviews from competent ones decomposes a change in a ratio into a rate effect, a mix effect and an interaction. For a metric averaged over segments with share wi and rate ri:

ΔR = Σ wi Δri  +  Σ ri Δwi  +  Σ Δwi Δri

The first term is performance, the second composition, the third usually small; Bahipatra's quarter is the second swamping the first. Plans started held at 11,000, but the enterprise/mid-market split moved violently, because one retail chain — nineteen distribution centres, Bahipatra's second-largest account — paused its rollout on 29 September pending an automation tender.

Enterprise share fell from 54.5 to 29.1 per cent, shifting 25.4 points into a segment that completes sixteen points worse. Rate effect: 0.545 × 1.0 + 0.455 × 1.0 = +1.0. Mix effect: (−0.254 × 78.0) + (+0.254 × 62.0) = −4.1. Interaction: zero. Sum −3.1 against an observed −3.0 after rounding. Every point of the decline, and more, is composition.

Four steps are usually left implicit. Choose the segmentation before looking at the outcome, or record that you did not: a cut selected after seeing which one tells a clean story is a hypothesis fitted to its own evidence. Publish the residual as a number, since a page adding to exactly 100 per cent is concealing a forced fit. Separate mechanism from timing, because "it coincided with the release" and "we found the broken call in the logs" are different grades of evidence. And write the ask before the analysis, publishing it last.

Second-order effects

Three consequences of running reviews deserve naming. They create selection bias toward instrumented causes: the winning explanation is the measurable one, not the largest, and over a year this redirects the instrumentation roadmap toward whatever makes reviews easy to write. They raise the metric's salience, inviting optimisation against it — hence the expert habit of pairing every headline with a sibling that would deteriorate if the headline were gamed. And they are commitment devices whether they intend to be or not: an attribution offered tentatively in week 40 is quoted as settled fact in week 46.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions are checkable before the page is written.

C1: the movement is distinguishable from the metric's own variation. Bahipatra passes overwhelmingly at eight sigma; Roznamcha only marginally. Comparing 92.5 to 88.0 per cent on audit samples of four hundred each, the pooled proportion is 0.9025, the standard error of the difference √(0.9025 × 0.0975 × (1/400 + 1/400)) = 0.021, and the observed 4.5-point gap a z of about 2.15 — roughly a three per cent chance under the null. That is evidence, not proof, and a page saying "accuracy has fallen" without adding "we would see a gap this large about one time in thirty by chance" has overstated itself.

C2: there exists an action inside this room's control. Roznamcha passes: the room can gate auto-accept, roll back, or fund a larger audit. Bahipatra fails instructively. No engineering action addresses a customer's procurement pause — so the review is not pointless, it is addressed to the wrong body, and the product room's only legitimate ask concerns how the metric is defined.

C3: the cause is attributable by mechanism, not timing. Bahipatra can name the account, the date and the contract clause. Roznamcha can name the model version but cannot say which behaviour of v5 produces the error — a weaker claim that must be written as one.

C4: the decision is cheap to reverse. One page suits a reversible choice; for repricing, a restatement or a regulatory filing, it is a cover note and the full analysis must travel with it.

The review is actively misleading in three situations. When the metric is a ratio over a population whose composition is moving, as at Bahipatra, the headline is a statement about the customer base masquerading as one about the product. When the movement is a measurement change — new logging, a redefinition, a timezone boundary, a bot filter — any causal story is fabricated, and the honest page says the series is broken and gives the date from which it is comparable. And when the audience treats the page as the analysis rather than its summary, brevity becomes false confidence; the countermeasure is a line naming the underlying document and who can be cross-examined on it.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the hard part is ownership. A shared surface — a home screen, a notification budget — moves two products in opposite directions, and each review can be honest while the pair is collectively misleading. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than they claim: the stated mechanism is a portfolio review netting the effects; the actual one is a pre-meeting where two product leaders agree whose page carries the bad half.

Two-sided marketplaces break the single-headline convention outright. A blended transaction count can rise while the binding constraint worsens, because a fall in supply raises measured conversion among buyers who still find inventory. The disciplined form reports each side's rate and names which side is constrained; the test is whether the page can say in one sentence what would have to change, and on which side.

In regulated contexts — lending, insurance and payments under RBI, SEBI or IRDAI supervision — a written causal attribution becomes a record. A page saying "we believe the error rate rose after our September release" can be produced in a supervisory examination, which is why such firms' reviews read in a strangely evidential register. What mature firms actually do is separate the artefacts: an internal review that thinks freely in probabilistic language, and a controlled incident record stating only what is verified. Merging them makes the review less candid or the record less defensible.

Hardware-plus-software products move the denominator. Active users is the wrong base when fleets update at different rates; the unit is firmware-version cohort, and the reviewer must distinguish a real regression from the composition effect of a staged rollout. Siyaha Instruments, a Coimbatore maker of connected cold-chain loggers, spent a fortnight on a "reliability regression" that was entirely the arrival of a new hardware revision into the fleet.

AI-native products face Roznamcha's problem structurally. Behaviour changes when the model version changes, so the series has a version dimension most instrumentation lacks, and proxies like acceptance rate can move because output became more persuasive rather than more correct. Such a review needs a ground-truth channel — a human audit with a stated sample size — and that channel is a budget line someone must defend.

The sharpest seam is that finance and product routinely report different numbers for the same thing, because of date boundaries, revenue recognition or de-duplication rules. Firms that review well reconcile before the page circulates and state the convention on it; firms that review badly discover the discrepancy live, in front of the board, and spend the meeting on bookkeeping.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert

The residual is the product, not the embarrassment. The tell is a page saying "these causes account for 78 per cent of the fall; we cannot explain the remaining 22." The obvious reading — that full attribution signals rigour — is wrong: real movements have many small contributors, and a page assigning all of a change to one or two causes has absorbed the unexplained part into whichever was easiest to measure.

Composition before performance. An expert checks whether segment weights moved before whether rates moved, because mix effects are commercial news in product clothing. The tell is a reviewer who asks "did the customer base change?" before "did the funnel change?". The obvious reading — that a fall in a quality metric is a quality problem — is wrong whenever the metric averages a heterogeneous base, which is nearly always.

Confidence attaches to mechanism, not correlation. The tell is a page naming what would have changed the author's mind: "if the error rate had moved on accounts still on v4, this explanation would be wrong." The obvious reading — that stating confidence is hedging — inverts the truth. The falsifier is what lets a leader act decisively: it names which observation would require revisiting the decision.

The ask is a separate object with a price and a deadline. An expert's ask is not "support" but "two engineers for three weeks, decided by Friday, or the audit sample stays at four hundred." The tell is that it survives being read alone. The obvious reading — that a clear explanation implies its action — is wrong: several competent people each infer a different action, and the meeting ends in deferral.

The streetlight bias must be declared. Experts keep a list of causes they could not check, and say so: "we could not rule out a change in the partner bank's routing because we do not receive their error codes." The obvious reading — that unchecked hypotheses weaken the page — is wrong; naming them stops the checked ones being over-weighted.

Every ratio is shown as two series. An expert displays numerator and denominator separately, because many alarming ratio movements are denominator events. The tell is a reviewer who, shown a conversion drop, first asks how traffic moved. The obvious reading — that a rate is cleaner because it controls for volume — is wrong when the volume change is the news.

Reviews close loops before they explain. The tell is an expert who opens with last period's commitment and its outcome before this period's movement. The obvious reading — that new news deserves the front page — is wrong: a series that never revisits its past actions trains a room to treat every page as costless.

Explanations have a half-life, and experts measure their own. The rarest tell is a practitioner who tallies the causes they asserted over four quarters and how many survived; those who do typically find a survival rate between half and two-thirds. The obvious reading is that a low rate signals incompetence; in fact a rate near 100 per cent means the person was only asserting the already-known.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the metric is high-volume and noisy, so limits are tight and real signals are usually technical or channel-driven; segmentation by platform, app version and acquisition source is the most productive first cut. In B2B and enterprise the opposite holds: volumes are small, a handful of accounts dominate, and the review's arithmetic is concentration arithmetic — the page names the account, not the percentage, and the audience includes a revenue leader whose action is a customer conversation. Bahipatra is the pure form. Platforms and marketplaces require side-separated reporting and a named constraint; hardware inherits a physical lag, so the ask concerns a future cohort; for AI products, model version is a first-class dimension and a ground-truth audit is mandatory.

Stage matters in one direction only. Where the reader already has full context, the review compresses to two sentences in a chat thread and formality is waste; as organisational distance grows the one-page discipline becomes more valuable, not less, because the reader is further from the code and closer to the capital. What does not change with stage, despite being widely asserted to, is the underlying analysis: the decomposition a twenty-person company owes itself is the one a two-thousand-person company owes its board, and the claim that early teams can skip it because they "know their users" is an argument for skipping arithmetic.

8. Three worked cases

Vahikhata Bazaar, a Jaipur marketplace for handloom and craft producers, saw gross merchandise value rise four per cent in a month while its review team flagged a problem. Buyer-side conversion had risen from 3.1 to 3.6 per cent, which looked like improvement; but active sellers with inventory had fallen from 11,400 to 9,800, and queries returning fewer than five results had risen from 12 to 29 per cent. Conversion rose because scarcity concentrated demand onto surviving listings; the constraint was supply, so the ask was a seller-reactivation budget, not a checkout experiment. Three months later GMV turned down exactly as the page said it would if sellers did not recover — the strongest evidence a review can generate about itself.

Siyaha Instruments is the denominator case. A monthly review reported that the share of cold-chain loggers returning a full day of telemetry had fallen from 96.2 to 91.4 per cent, and a firmware rollback was proposed. Decomposition by hardware revision showed revision A holding at 96.3 across both months while revision B, newly shipped and now 21 per cent of the fleet, sat at 73 — a real defect, but in a new antenna assembly, not firmware. The rollback would have cost four weeks and fixed nothing. When a fleet's composition changes, the aggregate averages populations that did not exist in the prior period.

Rokadbahi Payments is the failure. Between August and September, monthly transacting users fell nine per cent, from 3.10 million to 2.82 million. The review attributed the fall to a competitor's cashback campaign, citing app-store rankings and a plausible timing overlap, and asked for a counter-campaign. Leadership approved ₹14 crore. Three weeks later a support engineer traced the real cause: a September SDK change had broken the UPI intent handoff on one Android manufacturer's skin, covering 22 per cent of the base. The campaign was pouring spend into a funnel structurally broken for one user in five; blended acquisition cost rose from ₹310 to ₹1,140.

Three things made the failure possible and only one was analytical. The review named an external cause before ruling out the company's own releases — the cheapest check available, skipped because nobody owned it. It stated the share of the fall in words rather than numbers, so nobody noticed they did not add up. And it offered no residual, removing the prompt to ask what else was happening. The recovery was procedural: no review may name an external cause until the period's change log has been walked and initialled; per-OEM monitoring was added; attributions must be percentages that sum. The ₹14 crore did not come back.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The most common failure is narrating noise. The warning is a review series in which every week has a cause; the diagnostic is "what is this metric's standard deviation over twenty weeks?"; caught late, the cost is a quarter reorganising around explanations of randomness, and a room that no longer recognises real signals.

The second is attribution without a residual, as at Rokadbahi. The warning is causal language without percentages; the diagnostic is "what share does this account for, and what is the rest?" Caught late, capital is committed against a story and the organisation learns the wrong lesson about its market.

The third is the aggregate that averages incompatible populations. The warning is a ratio over a base whose composition nobody reports; the diagnostic is "did the weights move?" Caught late, a board governs by a number that has stopped measuring what it was chosen to measure — Bahipatra's exposure.

The fourth is proxy drift, Roznamcha's case, where the measured and the valued thing separate. The warning is a metric improving while the complaint channel worsens; the diagnostic is "when did we last verify this proxy against ground truth?" Caught late in a regulated business, the cost is not a metric but an examination.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether most movements deserve explanation at all. The control position holds that a weekly review should usually report nothing, and that the demand for weekly narrative causes most bad product decisions; its evidence is Deming's funnel and the observation that retrospectively "explained" weekly movements rarely replicate. The narrative position holds that writing forces understanding silence never produces, and that organisations which stop explaining stop noticing. Control is wrong if noise carries early signal — if small movements reliably precede large ones. Narrative is wrong if the cost of manufactured explanations exceeds the option value of the occasional early catch. Neither is settled.

Whether confidence language belongs on the page. The calibration camp holds that unqualified attributions are how bad decisions get made confidently, citing forecasting research that explicit probability improves accuracy over time. The decisiveness camp — strongest in cultures descended from Grove and Bezos — holds that leaders already discount what they read, that hedged pages get discounted twice, and that the real protection is fast reversal rather than a careful adjective. Calibration fails if leaders ignore stated confidences, which some evidence suggests; decisiveness fails wherever reversal is expensive, which is where stakes are highest.

Whether the ask belongs in the same document as the analysis. The advocacy objection is real: an author who knows what they will ask for is motivated to find supporting evidence, and a growing minority separate a findings memo from a proposal. The counter is that separation doubles the meetings and hides the advocacy rather than removing it. The usual compromise — write the ask first for yourself, write the analysis as if you did not know it, then check whether it still supports the ask — is a discipline, not a solution.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this writes a well-structured page. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently before the page exists. They know the standard deviation of their principal metrics without looking, and will decline to write a review. They reach for composition before performance and the denominator before the ratio. They write the ask first and publish it last, and state their falsifier unprompted. They open a review by closing the previous one, and keep a private hit rate on their own attributions, unembarrassed that it is not high. And when the analysis shows that the metric the room governs by is the wrong metric — the hardest version of this job — they say so on the page rather than quietly proposing a better one three months later.

12. What each protagonist decided

Nandita's page led with a sentence the CRO had not expected: plan completion improved in both segments, and the company-wide fall is entirely composition, driven by one account's rollout pause. She showed Table 1 and the waterfall, disclosed a residual of 0.1 points, and made two asks. The first, addressed to the CRO, was a named escalation on the paused account, with a date. The second was harder — that the board deck replace the blended completion rate with a fixed-weight index, holding segment shares at their trailing-four-quarter average, so the governing metric measures product performance rather than sales mix. She proposed reporting both rather than dropping the blended figure, which remains an honest description of what the installed base experiences. Her reasoning: a metric a board governs by must be attributable to someone's actions, and a blended ratio over a shifting base is attributable to no one.

Aakash rolled back nothing. His page stated that acceptance was up seven points, that audited accuracy of accepted records was down 4.5 points on a sample of four hundred, that a gap this large would arise by chance about one time in thirty, and that the combination implied roughly 4,100 wrong-and-unedited records a week against about 2,300 before — the number that made the room sit up, because it was in records rather than percentages. He could not name the mechanism, and said so. He disabled automatic acceptance for the two record types with the highest downstream cost, crop-loan disbursement and claim intimation, leaving v5 in place elsewhere; his ask was a standing budget to raise the weekly audit from four hundred records to twelve hundred, making a difference of this size detectable in one week rather than three. His falsifier was on the page: if the next audits showed accuracy recovering on the gated types while ungated types held, the effect was confidence-driven acceptance rather than model quality, and the remedy was interface design, not rollback.

Three questions for discussion. First: Nandita's fixed-weight index makes the metric attributable but less representative of what customers experience — when is a less accurate number the better governing number? Second: Aakash acted on evidence at roughly the three per cent level with no established mechanism; had the sample been one hundred rather than four hundred and the gap identical, what should he have done differently, and does the answer depend on the regulator? Third: Rokadbahi's review was well written, clearly argued and wrong — which discipline in section 3 would have caught it, and what would a year of that discipline have cost?

13. Going deeper

Root cause analysis of a metric change is the document this page reports; mastering it makes a one-page attribution defensible rather than plausible. Communicating with leadership supplies the theory of the audience — what a room absorbs and what it does with ambiguity. Data storytelling for decisions is the next and more dangerous step: how a chosen framing of a true number changes the decision a room reaches. Constructing a funnel gives the decomposition its skeleton, and reading drop-off teaches which step losses are pathological and which are selection working correctly. Defining activation matters because most disputed reviews are disputes about what counts as a user. Cohort analysis separates composition from performance, the central skill here. Retention curves and the PMF signal supply the baseline against which a movement is judged large or small, and stickiness and natural frequency explain why a week is the wrong review window for some products and far too long for others.

Kasturi Foods: One Page for Monday

Mumbai, Sunday 20 September 2026. A quarterly business review at half past nine, a chief executive who has asked for a single page, and six exhibits that do not agree about what happened, why, or whether it matters.

1. The night before

Meher Chitnis had been told the format three weeks earlier and had not, until Sunday evening, understood that the format was the difficulty. Yogesh Karnik wanted one page. Not a deck, not an appendix: one page, projected, containing what happened to the direct business in the quarter just closed, why it happened, what the team intended to do, and what it needed from the board. He had said it twice in July and once, more sharply, in an all-hands in August, after a forty-one-slide review that had run ninety minutes and produced no decision.

It was now ten past ten at night in Prabhadevi. Meher's flat looked across at the mill chimney that the developers had preserved and lit, and she had been staring at it more than at the screen. On the screen was a page. It had a heading, four sections, three numbers in bold, and one chart. She had rewritten it eleven times since Friday and each version had been true in a different way.

The facts that would not fit together were simple to state. In the quarter just ended, Kasturi Foods' direct-to-consumer revenue had grown 9 per cent over the previous quarter, which was below plan but not alarming. Ninety-day repeat purchase rate had fallen from 38 per cent to 27 per cent, which was alarming. Contribution margin per direct order had fallen from ₹64 to ₹19, which was, in Aparna Sule's phrasing on Friday, catastrophic. And quick commerce — Kasturi's tins and pouches on Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart — had grown 61 per cent in the same quarter with no product investment at all.

The board pack was due at midnight. Meher had written eleven versions of one page because there were at least four defensible accounts of the quarter, and the choice among them was not a writing problem. It was a claim about what Kasturi Foods was becoming, and she was going to make it in about two hundred words, in front of the person who had built the company, with a strategic investor's representative in the room as an observer.

2. How Kasturi was built

Kasturi Foods was founded in Mumbai in 2019 by Yogesh Karnik, a third-generation trader from a Dadar wholesale family, and his co-founder Sarita Gokhale, a food technologist from CFTRI. The product was baked and roasted Indian snacks — chiwda, bhakarwadi, millet-based namkeen, jowar puffs — positioned against the fried mainstream. The company sold first through its own website, then through Amazon and Flipkart, then into modern trade, and from late 2022 into quick commerce, which by FY26 was its fastest-growing channel. Revenue in FY26 was ₹214 crore. The company was EBITDA-negative by ₹27 crore.

The decision that constrains the present was taken in February 2024. Kasturi had raised a Series B on a direct-to-consumer thesis, and the investors had wanted proof that the brand owned its customer. Yogesh committed to building a first-party consumer platform: an app, a loyalty programme called Kasturi Club, a subscription for monthly staples, and a consumer data platform that would stitch the app, the website, the WhatsApp channel and, eventually, the QR codes printed on pack. The commitment was made publicly in the fundraise announcement and privately in a board resolution that authorised ₹14 crore a year of direct-business operating expenditure — product, engineering, performance marketing and the CDP licence — with a review at the end of FY27.

Two consequences followed. The first was organisational: the direct business became a separate P&L with its own marketing budget, which meant that every rupee spent acquiring a direct customer was visible, while the trade spend that bought shelf position at DMart or a slot on a quick-commerce home page sat inside the brand marketing line and was never allocated to a channel. The second was contractual: the CDP was licensed on a three-year deal, ending March 2027, with an annual fee of ₹1.9 crore and a clause requiring twelve months' notice of non-renewal. That notice period expired in March 2026 without anyone acting on it, so FY28 is already committed.

3. The industry around it

By 2026 the Indian packaged-snacks market had three distinct competitive layers and Kasturi sat awkwardly between them. At the top were Haldiram's, Bikaji and Balaji Wafers, with distribution reaching a scale no venture-funded brand could approach and pricing power to match. In the middle were the health-adjacent challenger brands — Too Yumm, Open Secret, Farmley, ITC's Yoga Bar — competing for the same urban consumer as Kasturi on the same shelves and the same quick-commerce search terms. Below both was general trade, where Kasturi had presence in roughly 31,000 outlets in Maharashtra and Gujarat, mostly through two distributors.

Three external forces pressed on the quarter under review. The first was the FSSAI's revised front-of-pack labelling requirement, which had forced a pack redesign across the portfolio through the first half of 2026; the redesign cost ₹2.1 crore in artwork, plates and obsolete laminate, and the new packs had reached quick commerce before they reached general trade. The second was edible-oil and millet input cost, which had moved unhelpfully through June and July, and which the company had answered with a 6 per cent price increase on eleven stock-keeping units effective 1 July — implemented immediately on the direct channel, where Kasturi controlled the price, and with a five- to seven-week lag in trade, where the pipeline had to clear. The third was quick commerce itself: platform commissions, advertising rates and the cost of remaining visible on a crowded category page had all risen, and none of that cost appeared in Kasturi's direct-business P&L.

Kasturi's exposure outside India ran through two doors. Rayyan Foodstuff Trading in Dubai had distributed Kasturi into Gulf retail since 2023 and now took about ₹11 crore a year, its buyers valuing the long shelf life of the baked range. Nikhil Bhende, working from Edison, New Jersey, sold into North American ethnic grocery, a smaller but higher-margin book. 4. What happened, in order

1 July 2026. The 6 per cent price increase went live on the direct channel. In trade and quick commerce, old-price stock continued to sell through until mid-August.

2 September 2026. The data team restated order-level cost of goods for the whole of FY27 to date, after discovering that freight-in had been allocated at a standard rate that had not been updated since FY25. 11 September 2026. Aparna Sule circulated a note proposing that direct-business operating expenditure be cut from ₹14 crore to ₹6 crore in FY28 and that the team be folded into brand marketing.

At eleven o'clock Meher opened a twelfth version and typed a heading she had not used before: What we got wrong about our own numbers. She looked at it for a while and then did not write anything under it.

The difficulty was not that she lacked an account of the quarter. She had four, and each of them was true enough to survive twelve minutes. The difficulty was that the page she wrote would be the page the company believed for a quarter, possibly longer, and that whichever of the four she chose would determine which of the others nobody looked at again. The Data Review for Leadership

What happened, why, what we'll do, what we need — on one page. The discipline that turns a root-cause analysis into a decision leadership can act on in a ten-minute meeting.

1. A Monday morning in Bengaluru

At 8:40 on a Monday in March, Priya Deshmukh, VP of Product at Taraazu, a Bengaluru-based expense-tracking and savings app with roughly 480,000 daily active users, opened a blank document titled "Leadership Data Review — Week 11." She had forty minutes before the 9:30 leadership sync, and one job: explain to Arjun Mehta, Taraazu's CEO, and the two other people in that room why daily active users had fallen from 480,000 to 437,000 over the previous seven days — a drop of 43,000 users, or just under nine percent — and what she intended to do about it. She already had the underlying analysis. Her data analyst, Rohan Iyer, had spent Thursday and Friday tracing the fall to a botched Android SDK upgrade that silently broke push notifications for a third of the user base. What she did not yet have was a version of that analysis that Arjun could read in ninety seconds and act on immediately, rather than one that required him to follow her reasoning through six intermediate steps. The gap between those two documents — the full investigation and the one page a leader can use — is the subject of this reading.

The stakes were not abstract. Taraazu was seven weeks from a board meeting where Arjun would present growth numbers to investors, and a rival app, Kaanta, had just closed a funding round on the strength of a similar user base. If Priya's review buried the headline under methodology, or overstated her confidence in the cause, or explained the problem without naming what she needed from the room, she would either lose the meeting to confusion or spend the next two weeks re-litigating a decision that should have taken ten minutes.

2. The idea

A data review for leadership is a single page, written for a specific decision-making audience, that answers four questions in order: what changed, why it changed, what the team will do about it, and what the team needs from the people in the room to do that. It is a distinct artifact from a dashboard, which shows numbers without an argument, and from a root-cause analysis (RCA) — the deeper investigative document, discussed elsewhere in this graph, that traces a metric movement to its mechanism. The review does not repeat the RCA; it reports its conclusion. The habit of structuring communication this way has no single inventor, but it converges on two older traditions: Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle, developed at McKinsey in the late 1960s, which insists that a document lead with its answer and only then supply supporting evidence; and the discipline Amazon popularized in the mid-2000s of replacing slide decks with short narrative memos read in silence at the start of a meeting. Product and analytics teams fused these into the now-common "what/why/what next/what we need" template sometime in the 2010s, as digital products generated more metrics than any executive had time to interpret unassisted. The sentence Priya could say in the room without sounding glib was this: "DAU is down nine percent, three-quarters of it is one Android bug we've already fixed, and I need two more engineering weeks to make sure it can't recur."

Fig. 1 — Taraazu's DAU across week 11. The line is flat until the Thursday SDK upgrade, then steps down and holds through the weekend until the fix ships the following Monday. The shape of the line is itself an argument: a sudden step, not a gradual slide, points to a single triggering event rather than a slow erosion of engagement.

3. How the review is actually built

Priya's forty minutes followed a sequence experienced analysts do largely from habit, which is precisely why newcomers skip steps without noticing. First, she confirmed the headline number was real and stable, not an artifact of a logging gap or a timezone boundary — a five-minute sanity check that catches a surprising share of false alarms before they reach a leadership deck. Second, she separated the metric movement into segments that might behave differently: platform (Android versus iOS), acquisition channel, and tenure (new users versus users active for 90 days or more). This segmentation is the step practitioners most often leave implicit, presenting a single aggregate number as if it were homogeneous when it rarely is. Third, she matched the timing of the movement against a change log of everything the company shipped that week, which is how Rohan had first noticed that the drop's onset lined up, to the hour, with the Android SDK release. Fourth, she quantified how much of the total drop each candidate cause explained, rather than stopping at "we think it's the SDK" — a review that names a plausible cause without a number attached invites exactly the follow-up questions it should pre-empt. Fifth, she translated the finding into an action already taken, with an owner and a date. Sixth, she wrote the "ask" — the one thing she needed from the room, stated as a decision or a resource. Only after these six steps did she write the page itself, which is why it reads as effortless: the effort happened earlier.

4. The worked example

The arithmetic behind Priya's headline is short enough to walk through in full. Total DAU fell from 480,000 to 437,000, a drop of 43,000 users, or 8.96 percent — she rounded this to "nine percent" in the review, since false precision on the second decimal buys nothing. Segmenting that drop by platform and by notification status produced three groups, shown in Table 1: Android users who normally received push notifications, whose DAU fell from 210,000 to 178,000, a drop of 32,000; iOS users, whose DAU fell only from 150,000 to 149,000, a drop of 1,000, well within ordinary noise; and non-push, direct-open users on both platforms, whose DAU fell from 120,000 to 110,000, a drop of 10,000, which Rohan attributed to a broader seasonal dip during a regional festival week rather than to the SDK bug.

The arithmetic that mattered for the meeting was 32,000 divided by 43,000: 74.4 percent of the drop was explained by one bug, already fixed, and the remainder was a seasonal pattern Taraazu had seen in the same week the previous year. That is the sentence "three-quarters of it is one Android bug" made precise. A second pass shows why the review also had to mention detection speed. The bug had run for three days before Rohan's Friday alert caught it; had the team's monitoring flagged it after one day instead of three, the affected population would have been roughly a third as large, since the notification failure compounded daily as more silently-updated devices went dark. Recomputing the Android segment at one day's exposure gives an estimated drop of about 10,700 users rather than 32,000, which would have made the week's total decline about 21,700, or 4.5 percent, rather than nine. Priya included this second calculation not to excuse the miss but to make the real ask legible: the fix that mattered most was not the notification patch itself but cutting detection time, which is what her request for two engineering weeks was actually for.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

A review is not a shorter RCA

Compressing an RCA is not the same exercise as writing a review. An RCA optimizes for completeness — every hypothesis considered and ruled out. A review optimizes for decision speed and deliberately discards hypotheses that were tested and rejected, keeping only the one that survived and a number attached to it.

One page is a discipline, not a length trick

The constraint forces a choice among causes even when reality has more than one contributing factor, as Taraazu's week did. Choosing the dominant cause and naming the residual honestly — "and a smaller seasonal effect we expect to reverse" — is harder than listing every factor at equal weight, and it is the actual skill being exercised.

Confidence must be calibrated, not performed

Saying "we're confident this was the SDK bug" when the evidence is a strong correlation over three data points overstates certainty. The honest form states the mechanism (notification delivery failure, verified in logs) and separates it from the correlation (timing alignment), because leadership will later ask what would have changed your mind.

The "ask" is a separate object from the explanation

Many reviews explain thoroughly and ask for nothing, leaving leadership to guess what response is wanted. An explanation without an ask produces a meeting that ends in "let's take this offline," which is where decisions go to be delayed.

What it cannot tell you

A one-page review cannot establish causal certainty from a single natural event; it reports the best available explanation, not a proven one. It also cannot substitute for the underlying RCA when the audience needs to inspect method, and it should say so rather than imply the page is the whole investigation.

Confused with a postmortem

A postmortem is blameless and technical, written for the engineering team that will prevent recurrence. A leadership review is business-facing and forward-looking, written for people who will decide about resources, targets, or external communication. The two documents share a root cause but almost nothing else in structure or audience.

Timing changes what the page needs to do

A review delivered before leadership has noticed the metric move can lead with explanation. One delivered after they have already seen a dashboard and formed a theory must first correct or confirm that theory, or it reads as if it is dodging the question they actually have.

The audience determines the ask's scope

A review written for a CEO can request an internal resourcing decision; the same review reused for a board update must instead frame the ask as a risk disclosed and a mitigation underway, since a board is not the body that allocates engineering weeks.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In a consumer app like Taraazu, the headline metric is almost always DAU, MAU, or a retention cohort, the cadence is weekly, and causes are frequently technical or channel-driven, as in Priya's case — which makes segmentation by platform and acquisition source the first and most productive cut. In a B2B product, the equivalent review looks different because the metric is often driven by a small number of large accounts: a usage dip can be one enterprise customer's procurement freeze rather than a systemic problem, so the review must name the account, not just the percentage, and the audience typically includes a sales or customer-success leader whose ask is a specific customer call, not an engineering sprint. In a marketplace, a single aggregate number can hide opposite movements on each side, so the review must report supply and demand separately and name whether the constraint is sellers, buyers, or the matching between them — a blended "transactions" figure misleads more often than it clarifies. Company stage matters as much as product type. At an early-stage company with one leadership figure who already has full context, the review can be a two-line chat message, since the audience needs no framing. At a large organization, the same finding must be legible to leaders several layers removed from the code and free of internal jargon — the one-page discipline matters more, not less, as that distance grows.

7. Common mistakes

Leading with process instead of the headline

Symptom: leadership interrupts within the first thirty seconds to ask "so what actually happened." Underlying misunderstanding: treating the review as a report of the work done rather than a report of what changed. Diagnostic: read the first sentence of the draft aloud — if its subject is "we" rather than the metric, rewrite it.

Reproducing the full RCA on the page

Symptom: the room's eyes glaze over at the third technical term, then someone asks a question the page already half-answered two paragraphs earlier. Underlying misunderstanding: conflating the investigative audience with the decision-making one. Diagnostic: hand the draft to someone outside the investigation and see whether they can repeat the cause back in a single sentence.

No stated ask

Symptom: the meeting ends with "let's regroup on this," and the same numbers resurface unresolved the following week. Underlying misunderstanding: believing that a clear explanation is self-executing. Diagnostic: check whether the page contains a sentence naming a decision, a resource, or a deadline — if it only contains findings, it is not yet a review.

False precision on causality

Symptom: leadership treats a hypothesis as settled fact, redirects a roadmap around it, and is later surprised when a second cause turns out to matter more. Underlying misunderstanding: presenting a strong correlation as a proven mechanism. Diagnostic: check for a stated confidence level or an explicitly named alternative explanation — its absence is the tell.

8. What good looks like

Three months later, a similar dip hit Taraazu's referral-driven signups. Priya's review that time was four short paragraphs: the number (signups down 14 percent week over week), the cause (a partner bank had throttled its API during a system migration, confirmed by a spike in a specific error code, not merely inferred from timing), the action (an engineer already routing around the throttled endpoint, live since the previous evening), and the ask (Arjun's approval to pause a planned campaign spend for one week rather than pour acquisition budget into a temporarily narrowed funnel). The meeting lasted six minutes. Arjun asked one clarifying question, approved the pause, and the group moved to the next agenda item. Nobody in the room needed to see the underlying RCA to trust the conclusion, because the review had already done the work of deciding what mattered and saying so plainly.

9. What Priya decided, and what comes next

Priya's finished review for week 11 led with the nine-percent number, attributed 74 percent of it to the Android notification bug with the mechanism named, disclosed the seasonal residual honestly rather than folding it into the same explanation, reported the fix as already shipped, and asked for two further engineering weeks to shorten detection time rather than to fix anything further about the notification bug itself. Arjun approved the ask in the first four minutes of the meeting and spent the remaining six asking about the board narrative, which the review had also anticipated. The reasoning behind Priya's choice was not that the seasonal explanation was unimportant, but that naming two causes with confidence would have cost more clarity than it purchased in accuracy; the residual was disclosed, not analyzed, because analyzing it was not this week's job. The natural next step in this graph is data storytelling for decisions, which asks a harder question than the review does: not merely what happened and why, but how a chosen framing of a true number can change which decision a room reaches — and how to guard against choosing a framing because it is convenient rather than because it is honest. Two questions worth sitting with before that reading: when you last explained a metric to a superior, did your first sentence name what changed or what you had done about it? And if a colleague read only your headline and your ask, skipping everything in between, would they still reach the same decision you wanted them to reach?

Nayaab Jewels: One Page for the Board

Weekly revenue is down fourteen per cent. Devika Rao has until Friday morning and a single sheet of paper.

1. Tuesday evening, Lower Parel

At twenty past eight on Tuesday 13 January 2026, Devika Rao was the only person left on the product floor of Nayaab Jewels' office in Lower Parel, Mumbai. On her screen were nine browser tabs, a shared spreadsheet from Toronto that had been updated forty minutes earlier, and an empty document titled Board update — weekly revenue.

The board met on Friday 16 January at half past nine. Ritu Sanghvi, Nayaab's chief executive, had sent Devika a message on Sunday that was friendly and entirely unambiguous: One page. What happened, why, what we'll do, what we need. Not the dashboard. I'll have eight minutes for it before we get to the funding round.

Devika had owned the purchase experience for two years. She had, by her own count, four candidate explanations for the fall in weekly revenue since the end of November, two of which were held with real confidence and two of which were not. She also had a growth head who wanted the page to say something quite different from what she believed it should say.

2. Nayaab Jewels

Nayaab Jewels sold fine jewellery online — gold chains and bangles, diamond studs, engagement rings, and a fast-moving "everyday gold" line of lightweight pieces aimed at salaried women in their late twenties. Founded in 2018 by two ex-merchandisers from the Zaveri Bazaar trade, it had grown to about ₹640 crore of annual revenue, roughly 1.4 lakh orders a year at an average order value of ₹46,000, and eleven experience studios in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Delhi NCR where customers could try pieces before buying online.

The market around it was crowded and formidable. Tanishq, from the Titan stable, and CaratLane defined the organised end; Kalyan Jewellers and Malabar Gold brought enormous regional trust; BlueStone and Giva competed hard on the lighter, lower-ticket pieces. Everyone operated under the same conditions: BIS hallmarking with unique identification on every article, three per cent GST, gold prices that had climbed roughly eleven per cent since September, and the Income-tax requirement that a permanent account number be recorded for jewellery transactions above ₹2 lakh.

Nayaab's team was deliberately distributed. Engineering sat in Pune under Kartik Joshi; the design lead, Anushka Sen, had moved to Berlin two years earlier and worked afternoons Indian time; the data science function was a team of three in Toronto; customer success for the Gulf and South-East Asian diaspora ran out of Singapore; and a two-person sales office in Edison, New Jersey handled the North American non-resident Indian market, which contributed nearly a fifth of revenue at almost double the domestic average order value.

3. What happened

On 28 November 2025, Nayaab shipped a revision to its checkout. The change was driven by finance and compliance: for any cart above ₹2 lakh, the customer was now asked for a PAN and a photograph of the card before proceeding to payment, rather than being asked for it after payment while the piece was being prepared for dispatch. The older flow had produced a steady trickle of orders that had to be held — sometimes for days — while the finance team chased documents, and in November the operations head had finally lost patience.

Weekly net revenue, which had averaged ₹11.8 crore in the four weeks before the festive season, ran at ₹10.1 crore, ₹9.9 crore, ₹9.6 crore and ₹10.15 crore in the four weeks that followed. Order volume was down less than revenue, which meant the shortfall was concentrated in the high-value end.

The views from around the company diverged predictably with geography. Kartik in Pune had, almost by accident, preserved a ten per cent holdout on the old flow for two weeks before the release was fully ramped — a small, unglamorous fact that turned out to be the most valuable piece of evidence anyone had. Priyanka Nair, the data scientist in Toronto, had the decomposition ready but sent it with four paragraphs of caveats at 3 a.m. Mumbai time and was asleep whenever Devika wanted to argue about it. Wei-Ling Tan in Singapore reported that Rimaal Trading, Nayaab's Dubai distribution partner for co-branded festive collections, had paused its January catalogue while a VAT invoicing mismatch was resolved — a fact that had not reached anyone in Mumbai for three weeks. And Farhan Qureshi, the growth head, had been telling anyone who would listen that the whole thing was gold prices and the post-Diwali lull.

4. The people

Devika Rao, Senior Product Manager, Mumbai. Accountable for checkout and the purchase funnel. She believes the PAN step is the largest single driver and can prove it, but she also knows that the step exists because finance asked for it, and that saying so in front of the board puts her in opposition to the chief financial officer.

Sameer Kulkarni, Chief Financial Officer, Mumbai. He wants held orders and document-chasing eliminated; every held order ties up gold inventory at elevated prices and creates reconciliation work. He is not hostile to changing the flow, but he will not accept a change that puts a compliance obligation at risk, and he has asked for written counsel before anything moves.

Farhan Qureshi, Head of Growth, Mumbai. He wants ₹2 crore released for an Akshaya Tritiya campaign in April and has an interest in the board believing that revenue softness is seasonal and external rather than self-inflicted. His argument is not dishonest; gold prices really have risen, and last January really was weak.

Priyanka Nair, Data Scientist, Toronto. She has built the decomposition and is the only person who can certify the numbers. She is professionally uncomfortable with any statement stronger than the evidence supports, and her instinct is to present all four drivers as equally uncertain — which, Devika suspects, would leave the board unable to act on any of them.

5. Exhibits

6. The options

Option A: present the investigation. Take the board through the funnel, the holdout, the grammage mix and the seasonality comparison, and ask for two more weeks before recommending anything. The upside is that Devika commits to nothing she cannot defend and avoids a public disagreement with Sameer. The cost is that the board's eight minutes produce no decision, the PAN step keeps costing roughly ₹78 lakh a week, and the next review starts from the same place.

Option B: one page, one ask. Lead with the headline — fourteen per cent down, three-quarters of it explained, half of it self-inflicted — show Exhibits 2 and 3, and make a single request: authority to move PAN collection back to after payment authorisation and before invoice, subject to written counsel confirming the compliance position, plus ₹35 lakh to fix the VAT invoicing that has stalled Rimaal. The upside is a decision on Friday. The cost is that Devika must say, in front of the board, that a change finance sponsored has cost about ₹4 crore a quarter.

Option C: the external story plus a growth ask. Present the fall as gold prices and post-festive seasonality, note the checkout change as a minor contributor under review, and ask for the ₹2 crore Akshaya Tritiya budget. The upside is that it is comfortable, partly true, and unites Devika with Farhan. The cost is that it spends ₹2 crore to compensate for a ₹78 lakh-a-week problem that two weeks of Kartik's time could fix, and it will be exposed the moment anyone reads the holdout.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows revenue falling three times as fast as orders. What does that single fact rule out, and which of the four drivers in Exhibit 2 does it favour?

2. Priyanka wants every driver presented with equal uncertainty. What is she protecting, what would it cost the board, and how should confidence be expressed on a one-page review?

3. Option C is partly true. What exactly makes it the wrong page to write, and how would you know within a quarter that it had been wrong?

4. Write the four blocks of Devika's page — what happened, why, what we will do, what we need — in no more than 120 words. What did you have to leave out, and where does it go?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an exercise in the discipline of the leadership data review. The reviewer's job is not to display analysis; it is to convert a metric movement into a decision that only this room can make. The form is fixed for a reason — what happened, why, what we will do, what we need — and each block has a quality test. "What happened" must name a comparison basis: Devika's is the ₹11.80 crore four-week pre-festive baseline, and saying so pre-empts the objection that she has cherry-picked a peak. "Why" must decompose to the whole of the move, with a residual written down and confidence labelled, which is exactly what Exhibit 2 does. "What we will do" must attach an owner, a date and an expected effect in the same unit as the metric. "What we need" must be shaped like a decision — a price, a date and the consequence of saying no.

A well-reasoned answer starts from the divergence in Exhibit 1. Revenue down 14 per cent on orders down 4.7 per cent is a value problem, not a demand problem, and it immediately demotes the seasonality and gold-price stories from explanations of the fall to components of it. Exhibit 3 then supplies the mechanism, and the holdout Kartik preserved supplies the causal claim, which is why that driver is the only one in Exhibit 2 that can carry the word "confirmed" without argument.

One defensible path is Option B, with two amendments that make it survivable. First, Devika should pre-wire the page: send Exhibits 2 and 3 to Sameer on Wednesday, and frame the recommendation as solving his original problem — held orders and chased documents — by moving PAN collection to the point where the customer is already committed, rather than by removing it. The recommendation then arrives at the board with finance beside her rather than opposite her. Second, she should make the ask conditional in writing: implement on receipt of counsel's confirmation, with a stated fallback of a lighter in-cart PAN capture if counsel disagrees. That way the board is deciding on economics, not adjudicating a compliance question it is not equipped to settle on a Friday morning.

The same reasoning also disposes of Farhan's ₹2 crore. It may well be a good campaign; it is simply not an answer to this page. A review that spends marketing money to offset a self-inflicted funnel loss is the most expensive form of not reading your own exhibit.
